title: The Best Pop-Up Debate Prompt in my Repertoire (Valued Within Exercise)
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart shares what he calls his favorite classroom discovery of the '23-'24 school year: a simple Pop-Up Debate prompt template -- "What was the most interesting thing you learned in this unit?" -- used at the end of a learning progression. He explains this as a "Valued Within" exercise, distinct from teacher-driven Mini-Sermons, because it places responsibility for finding value in the material on students themselves rather than the teacher. He walks through the layered benefits: students first write individually (forcing evaluation of meaning and boosting retention), then debate publicly, hearing and arguing with classmates who are all operating from the shared assumption that the class actually contains interesting material. The piece functions as a practical, subject-agnostic template teachers can adapt with their own end-of-unit variations.
points: The prompt itself is deceptively simple -- "What was the most interesting thing you learned in this unit?" -- but Stuart argues its power lies in the embedded assumption that the class is inherently interesting, delivered without direct sermonizing.

He distinguishes Valued Within exercises from Mini-Sermons on the basis of who does the intellectual work: in Mini-Sermons the teacher asserts value; in Valued Within exercises, students construct it themselves.
Even the writing-only stage (before any debate) delivers real value, since evaluating "interestingness" forces students to engage with the meaning of course material, which Stuart ties to retention.

The Pop-Up Debate format compounds the effect: students not only articulate their own reasoning but hear and sometimes argue with every classmate's take, reinforcing the shared assumption that the material has value.
quotes: As you'll recall, Valued Within exercises are any activity that has students figuring out why the work of learning is valuable to them. Unlike Mini-Sermons, in which creating and communicating Value messages are my responsibility, Valued Within exercises place that responsibility where it must ultimately reside: in the hearts of students.
At the end of a learning progression (week, unit, semester, etc.), this is the prompt template you use: What was the most interesting thing you learned in this unit?

Do you see the sneaky assumption within these prompts? THIS CLASS IS ACTUALLY INTERESTING! But instead of sermonizing my students on this, I'm pointing their minds toward it by having them interpret course material through the lens of interest.

Students have to think back on what they've been studying and evaluate the interestingness of things. This gets them thinking about the meaning of the things they've learned about, which is a great boon to retention and understanding of the course material.
Students are hearing ALL of their classmates articulate what they found interesting, and maybe even ARGUING with one another about which things are most interesting.
